summary:
Syria's Penal Code criminalises the conduct a trans visitor may be read as engaging in. Article 520 of the 1949 code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" and carries up to three years' imprisonment; Article 517 covers public indecency. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that both provisions reach men and women alike, so a trans visitor is reachable under the same articles irrespective of legal sex marker or presentation.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Syria, LGBTI organisations cannot register, and no anti-discrimination protection exists in any field. The state's response to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, which removes the complaint route a visitor would otherwise have after an assault, a refusal of service or a document dispute.

Enforcement has fallen on private gatherings. PinkNews reported on 23 June 2010 that Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over the preceding weeks and arrested more than 25 men in the latest swoop, most charged with "homosexual acts" and others with drug offences; the charges also included encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. That 2010 crackdown is the most recent documented enforcement action in this record; no later raid is documented here.

Public expression has been squeezed. The region's only gay tour, running through Damascus and Aleppo, stopped operating, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus have been eradicated since the civil war began. Its organiser described the Aleppo and Damascus hammams that anchored the pre-2011 route as "a paradise for gay people" where "we never had any problems." Digital expression continues under cover: a campaign whose name means "one of you" began on Facebook in March 2020 and moved to Twitter, with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves by a faculty building, most using fake accounts for fear of being identified; responses ranged from defence to threats of blood before it faded amid COVID-19.

Violence has come from non-state armed actors as well as the state. A Human Rights Watch report of 16 April 2018, updated 30 August 2021, records that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, against 23 in Iraq and 3 in Libya; the same record notes that the Islamic State reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in the areas it controlled, an issue raised at the UN Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first discussion of LGBTQ concerns. Beatings and torture of LGBTQ people are documented, including attacks attributed to Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State. These are raw counts with no population denominator, and the inventory contains no trans-specific violence figure that could be compared with Syria's general homicide rate.

Political actors have endorsed harsher treatment. A Free Syrian Army member, Nasradeen Ahme, said he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals; the secular leader Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would say "no way" to gays claiming rights.

Official stigma shapes health care. In 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low; the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. Comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist.

Two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council, a closed session in 2015 co-sponsored by the United States and Chile, describing constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS; activists separately worked to draw the ISIS killings to the attention of the Security Council.

Reporting from Damascus on 11 October 2020 found homosexuality and "public decency" offences illegal, with a 36-year-old resident describing living "only in whispers" when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes. A GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025, working through an on-the-ground reporter network, investigated and found inaccurate a claim that LGBTQIA individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Rights Watch tallies rank jurisdictions by raw counts of claimed killings (Syria 16, Iraq 23, Libya 3 as of June 2016) with no population denominator, so the ordering reflects population and conflict intensity rather than per-capita risk to an individual.

Adjacent turbulence: the collapse of public LGBTQ life since 2011 is attributed in the record to the civil war rather than to a single statute, and the armed opposition figures quoted on harsher treatment belong to that conflict period.

In the diaspora, Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries on the basis of race, language, skin colour and religious background, which is a separate exposure from anything documented inside Syria.

Expression cases with no direct bearing on a visitor's legal position include Abdulrahman Akkad, a Syrian young man in Germany who came out publicly on Facebook in July 2017 under family pressure to marry against his will and whose case was raised in the German Parliament's 2020 human rights session, and the 2017 film Mr. Gay Syria, which follows two gay Syrian refugees rebuilding their lives.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same Articles 520 and 517 that reach visitors, with no legal gender recognition route and no registered LGBTI organisation through which to seek redress; no anti-discrimination protection exists in employment, services, housing or any other field.

The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational programme for youth in secondary schooling, but comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Prevalence was recorded at under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987.

Organising is possible only anonymously: the "one of you" campaign of March 2020 relied on fake accounts, and its participants faced threats of blood before it faded amid COVID-19. LGBTI organisations cannot register, so there is no domestic body able to receive a complaint.

Earlier literary expression includes Nizar Qabbani's 1971 poem "The Evil Poem," describing a relationship between two women.
outOfScopeNotes:
The EUAA Syria country-focus page on treatment by state, non-state and societal actors yielded no usable finding for this record; nothing from it is asserted here.

No trans-specific violence statistic appears anywhere in the inventory. The ISIS figures (at least 16 claimed killings as of June 2016; at least 30 reported executions raised at the UN Security Council in August 2015) are raw counts of alleged same-sex conduct with no denominator and no comparison to Syria's general homicide rate during the conflict, so they cannot be read as a rate of risk.

Recency is unresolved: the most recent documented enforcement action in this record is the 2010 party raids, and the most recent non-state killing tally closes in June 2016. Whether later enforcement or targeted killings occurred is not sourced here, and the absence of a later entry is not evidence that the conduct has stopped.

The health figures are historical snapshots (2005 ministry and NGO estimates, 2018 prevalence, reported cases through Q3 2019) and are not presented as the current position. Whether any penalty under Article 520 has been applied since 2010, and whether Articles 520 and 517 have been amended since the fall of the Assad regime, are not sourced in this inventory.
